mcqs.question: What does git actually store when you make a commit that only touches one file out of a hundred?
options: A diff of that one file against the previous commit
A compressed patch set covering every commit since the file was created
The full contents of only the changed file, with the other 99 marked as unchanged
A complete snapshot of the whole project tree, reusing stored blobs for the 99 unchanged files
mcqs.explanation: Git records a full tree snapshot per commit; the 99 unchanged files simply have their tree entries point at blobs already stored from a previous commit, so nothing is duplicated. Diff-based storage, and replaying a patch chain, is the CVS/SVN model git deliberately avoids.

mcqs.question: What is a git branch, mechanically?
options: A movable pointer to a single commit in the DAG
A full copy of the repository's files at the point it was created
A diff between two commits stored as a named object
A permanent snapshot that never changes once created
mcqs.explanation: A branch is just a label pointing at one commit hash, which git slides forward on each new commit made while that branch is checked out. It copies no files. The "never moves" description fits a tag, not a branch.

mcqs.question: You edit a file, then run `git add` on it, then edit it again without staging the second change. What does `git commit` (with no flags) actually commit?
options: Whatever the file currently looks like on disk, including both edits
Nothing, because the file has unstaged changes
Only the version of the file that was staged after the first edit
The version from HEAD, since staging was never finalized
mcqs.explanation: Commit always commits the staging area's content, not the working directory's — that's the whole point of having an index. The second, unstaged edit stays as a pending working-directory change after the commit, visible in `git status` and `git diff`.

mcqs.question: Why does amending even the message of an old commit change the hash of every commit after it?
options: Git recalculates all hashes nightly as part of garbage collection
A commit's hash is derived from its content including its parent's hash, so changing any ancestor changes every descendant's hash too
It doesn't — only the amended commit's own hash changes
Because file contents are re-hashed whenever any metadata in the repo changes
mcqs.explanation: Since each commit's ID is a hash over its tree, parent pointer, author, and message, altering an ancestor produces a new hash for it, which changes what the child commit points to and thus the child's own hash — cascading forward. Nothing recalculates on a timer, and the effect is not limited to the amended commit itself.

mcqs.question: Right after `git add file.py`, you run `git diff` and see no output for that file. What's the correct next command to see what you just staged?
options: git diff --staged
git diff again, since it should have shown the change
git log -p
git status --diff
mcqs.explanation: Plain `git diff` compares working directory to the index, and `git add` just made those identical for this file — so empty output is correct, not a bug. `git diff --staged` compares the index to HEAD, which is exactly where the staged change now lives.

mcqs.question: A teammate commits an API key, then immediately commits a second change deleting it from the file. Is the secret safe once both commits are pushed?
options: Yes, since the current working tree and latest commit no longer contain it
Yes, as long as the deleting commit happens within the same day
No — the key still exists in the earlier commit's blob and is fetchable by anyone who has the repo, so it must be rotated
No, but only until the next `git gc` runs, which removes it automatically
mcqs.explanation: The blob holding the key is still reachable from the earlier commit and ships to every clone; deleting it later only changes the latest snapshot, not history. `git gc` prunes unreachable objects, but this blob is still reachable from a real commit, so gc never removes it — rotating the credential is the only real fix.
